title: Ben Berman - Machine Learning and Level Generation
speaker: Ben Berman
summary: Ben Berman surveys machine learning approaches to level generation (texture synthesis/wave function collapse, recurrent neural networks, MCMC design) framed by a trade-off between how much data you have and how much you tell the computer about what matters. He argues the main objective for ML level generation should be making content that looks hand-made rather than computer-made, which in practice means symmetry, pacing and small human-readable numbers rather than difficulty as the core parameter. He then gives practical advice for training character-level RNNs on levels: treat levels as 1D sequences, rip data from existing games via modding tools, beware buggy public implementations, re-encode tiles semantically, and denoise output. He closes by pointing to functional game content (e.g. generated card/monster behaviour) as the next frontier.

insights.claim: Machine learning methods for content generation trade off between needing lots of data and needing the designer to tell the computer what is important.
insights.detail: Berman frames the whole field as this trade-off: methods like character RNNs give only a broad intuition but need a lot of data, while NLP grammars work on tiny corpora because the rules are specified. Methods that both discover what matters and need little data (strong AI) do not exist yet.
insights.quote: if you want to do this well you need either a lot of data or there's some methods that use very little data

insights.claim: Heuristic roguelike level generators are a special case of Monte Carlo Markov chain design, where the generator keeps trying until output fits designer-specified measures such as symmetry or good room layout.
insights.detail: MCMC design lets you specify properties you know matter, e.g. a level should be symmetric, and keeps generating until outputs fit those measurements. Berman says every heuristic roguelike generator is a hand-decided version of this rather than the computer figuring out the criteria.
insights.quote: every single roguelike today that uses heuristic level generation is really special case of Monte Carlo Markov chain design

insights.claim: A character-based recurrent neural network trained on text representations of Super Mario levels produced plausible, playable levels without knowing anything about jumping or difficulty.
insights.detail: Berman cites Adam Summerville's UCSC research: the network only assumed that later parts of a level relate to earlier parts. He notes the shown output was probably curated.
insights.quote: it didn't know anything about the rules and know anything about jumping or difficulty it just kind of looked at a bunch of Mario levels

insights.claim: Neural-network character animation trained on motion capture can generate film-quality movement from controller input alone and can react to generated heightmap terrain.
insights.detail: Berman argues more accessible roguelikes require thinking critically about art. The demo used about 30 hours of motion capture and was made by three people; the character climbs stairs and runs into walls of a heightmap world, which he says could be used in a game today.
insights.quote: if you want to make more accessible roguelikes you have to start thinking about art very critically nobody animated this

insights.claim: MCMC methods let a designer guide generated detail, such as refining a blocked-out spaceship or laying out furniture in a room using interior design logic.
insights.detail: Berman shows Daniel Ritchie's work: a coarse spaceship becomes a detailed one, and objects placed in a room are arranged prettily over time. He suggests this matters for non-tile 3D roguelikes where decorating rooms is hard.
insights.quote: decorating a room when you don't have tiles is really challenging there's actually software that can help you do that

insights.claim: The most productive goal for machine-learned level generation is making levels that look made by hand rather than by a computer.
insights.detail: Berman says this is how he has found success commercially, and contrasts it with heuristic generators whose output usually reads as computer-made. He repeats it as the mission at the end of the talk.
insights.quote: I really focus on making stuff that looks like it's made by hand not by a computer

insights.claim: Cloudberry Kingdom parameterised its generated platformer levels by difficulty, and the result obviously looks computer-made, so Berman recommends rejecting difficulty as the main generation parameter.
insights.detail: Berman praises the game's ambition (years of work) but notes its levels look machine-made. He argues roguelikes are hard enough already and cites zero-difficulty, fun-to-watch human-made Mario levels and the Sonic Adventure opening as aspirational examples.
insights.quote: making stuff that looks like a computer really means rejecting difficulty as your parameter you know roguelikes are already hard enough

insights.claim: Random, organic-looking placement signals procedural generation, while symmetry, pacing and regular features make tile-based levels feel handcrafted.
insights.detail: Berman contrasts a ball-dodging game whose randomly placed obstacles read as generated with things made by people, which tend to be symmetric and paced. He tells roguelike developers to use their tile grid to their advantage.
insights.quote: when things are made by people they tend to have symmetry they tend to have this this certain pay scene and kind of regular features

insights.claim: The Binding of Isaac uses mirrored room layouts to convince players its rooms were handcrafted.
insights.detail: Berman describes taking the left half of a room and flipping it; placing the rocks asymmetrically instead would not feel like a person made it. He says symmetry is simple to express in the ML techniques he discusses.
insights.quote: this is binding of issac which I think uses symmetry beautifully to convince you that these things were handcrafted

insights.claim: Small, single-digit numbers make game stats feel deliberately designed, while overly precise multi-digit numbers feel procedural or over-tuned.
insights.detail: Berman contrasts Clash Royale, whose three-digit numbers feel triangulated to stiff the player, with Hearthstone, whose one-digit card stats make players feel a human thought about each one.
insights.quote: in this game numbers have one digit and you feel like there's a lot of important consideration

insights.claim: Modelling a roguelike level as a one-dimensional sequence, like a platformer where time moves you forward, opens it up to almost every machine learning tool.
insights.detail: Summerville's Mario generator assumed you only go forward and it worked. For 2D games like The Binding of Isaac, Berman suggests expressing a 2D level as multiple 1D levels plus a small heuristic tweak.
insights.quote: you got to think of it as a 1d platformer all you make is a decision to go left or right and time kind of brings you forward

insights.claim: Training data for level generators can be ripped from existing games through modding-community tools rather than collected at great expense.
insights.detail: Berman says he tried extracting data from five or six games and succeeded for all of them. A model trained on raw hexadecimal Geometry Dash levels produced levels that could be pasted into the game and played.
insights.quote: you can rip data from existing games you know don't necessarily commit yourself to the multi hundred million dollar project

insights.claim: Many public implementations of character RNNs contain subtle bugs, so failed experiments may be due to broken code rather than the method.
insights.detail: Berman cites a Python array-duplication bug (references instead of copies) present in widely used code for months. People who tried such code may have wrongly concluded the approach could not work.
insights.quote: stuff is super buggy online it's really really crazy how many of these implementations are totally objective roken

insights.claim: Reading a tile level in a snaking path order rather than naive chunks greatly improved RNN-generated Mario levels, likely because it helps the network learn to count tiles.
insights.detail: UCSC research found snaking along tiles gave better results than the uneven chunking of off-the-shelf code. In Q&A Berman speculates that it lets the network count runs (e.g. six sky tiles) before deciding to place something.
insights.quote: I think sneaking helps it count and that's probably the the core part of why this little innovation

insights.claim: Re-encoding level tiles into semantic categories such as passable, interactable and reward, and recording where categories change, makes rare features learnable by neural networks.
insights.detail: Berman shows a Mario level as binary layers; rewards like coins are too rare to learn amid empty space. Recording column switches multiplies the number of ones, a form of convolution that also lets you train across multiple games.
insights.quote: I'm gonna categorize my tiles and I say they're passable tiles they're interactable tiles or reward tiles

insights.claim: Generated levels are noisy, and treating the level like an image to denoise it, e.g. pushing stray blocks to walls or mirroring halves, yields architecturally cohesive output.
insights.detail: Berman says noise is the biggest problem: random blocks break rules of architecture. He suggests dragging stray bricks against walls then turning them into bookcases, or tweaking the left half to match the right to both remove noise and add symmetry.
insights.quote: I think the biggest problem is noise you know you you generate this stuff and if it isn't a human being curating it

insights.claim: Generating functional game content, such as monster behaviours or playable Hearthstone-like cards, is the next frontier beyond generating level layouts.
insights.detail: Berman says a Hearthstone card is really a roguelike monster in disguise, and currently designers must hand-write monster behaviour. He has been experimenting with generating functional cards and calls it the future for the next five to ten years.
insights.quote: a hearthstone card is really just a monster and we're in a roguelike in disguise like the way that it behaves

insights.claim: A pity system guarantees a good item after many failed random draws, making the gambler's fallacy actually true in the game.
insights.detail: Answering a question, Berman explains that after e.g. 40 failed attempts the system gives an awesome item anyway. He warns this can be highly addictive for people with gambling problems.
insights.quote: if you didn't unpack an awesome item after trying 40 times the system feels pity for you and gives you an awesome item anyway

insights.claim: Influential computer-generated content usually relies on human curation, and reaching a high hit rate without curation is the hard open problem.
insights.detail: Asked whether players are simply getting used to algorithmic content, Berman says impressive examples hide that 99% of output may not feel human-made. He concedes players accept randomly placed obstacles in popular games and roguelikes, calling it a complicated question.
insights.quote: if you want to hit that 99 percent performance level you have to think about you know like how am i curating
